content.text: Since 2012 | 10,000+ Items | 48 Hr Turnaround | Google Rating

children.text: What Is Powder Coat Stripping and Recoating?

Powder coat stripping and recoating is a two-part restoration process. The old finish comes off completely, then new powder is applied electrostatically and cured in an oven. The goal is a clean, even finish that bonds to bare metal instead of a new layer sitting on a failing one.

Powder coat recoating over a damaged finish rarely lasts. A peeling powder coat or a chipped powder coating usually means the bond has already failed, and a new coat on top can lift in the same places. Rust under the surface makes this worse, because it keeps spreading beneath any new film. That is why we remove the old finish first and complete surface rust treatment before the new powder goes on.

Not every part needs full powder coating restoration. A faded powder coat on a sound surface may only need cleaning and a refresh, while rust, damage or a colour change calls for complete old coating removal. We assess each part before we quote, so powder coat stripping and recoating covers only the work the part actually needs.
How Our Powder Coat Stripping and Recoating Process Works

Our powder coat stripping and recoating process has six stages: assessment, removal, rust repair, pretreatment, recoating and inspection. Each stage protects the next one, so the new finish bonds properly and lasts.

Assessment. We look at the metal, the existing coating, the extent of rust and any damage. Photos sent with your quote request help us plan the stripping and recoating, including the removal method, the repairs and the finish, before the part arrives.

Removal. We take the old finish down to bare metal. Paint stripping and powder coat stripping take different effort, so we confirm the method for your part when we quote. Heavy coatings, scale and rust often call for blasting, described on our
sandblasting services
page.

Rust repair. Surface rust is cleaned from the metal so it cannot spread under the new coat. Deep pitting or structural damage is flagged to you early, because recoating cannot restore a weakened part.
Pretreatment. Clean metal can develop flash rust quickly, so pretreatment before recoating follows removal closely. Our
surface preparation
page explains the washing and masking steps, and surface preparation for recoating is part of every restoration job.
Recoating. We plug threads and bores, then apply the powder electrostatically. Oven curing at 180–200 °C melts the powder into one continuous film.
Inspection. We check coverage, colour and finish, measure film thickness and look for defects before packing the part.

Timing matters as much as technique. Typical shop work follows our standard 48-hour turnaround, and we receive parts Monday to Friday, 7 AM to 5 PM. Planning powder coat stripping and recoating as one job keeps bare metal from sitting uncoated, which is the main cause of early flash rust. Recoating turnaround for larger or heavily rusted parts is confirmed when we quote. Parts with several layers of old paint can take longer to strip, so we ask for photos early.
Which Parts and Metals Can We Restore?
Our stripping and recoating service covers steel and aluminum parts that can withstand curing, from small brackets to large fabricated frames. See our
capabilities
page for size and weight limits. Typical jobs include:
Railings and gates. Railing restoration and gate restoration are common, because outdoor metalwork loses its finish first.
Equipment and machinery. Equipment refurbishment and machinery refurbishment bring worn housings, guards and frames back to a protected finish.
Structural steel and frames. Structural steel recoating suits fabricated frames and supports where rust has started under the old coat.
Older metalwork. Aging metalwork from churches, parks and buildings often carries several layers of old paint, which we remove before recoating.

Galvanized, cast and heavily welded parts can need extra checks because trapped gases may affect the surface, so tell us the material when you request a quote. Some parts are not worth restoring, and we will say so if the metal is too weak or too damaged. For parts that live outdoors, powder coat stripping and recoating helps restore weathered metal and extend coating life.
Restoration and Recoating Options
You can return a part to its original look or change it completely. The stripping and recoating options below cover the most common requests, and each can be paired with a new finish.
Like-for-like recoating. We aim for an original colour match so the restored part blends with the rest of the installation. Send a colour code, a RAL number or a small sample.
Colour change recoating. A new shade, sheen or texture gives older parts a new look. Our
custom powder coating colours
page explains the choices.
Removal with repair. Some parts need old coating removal and rust repair before they return to service. Tell us what is wrong and we will confirm the steps.
Repair or recoat. A small chip may be repairable, but widespread peeling, rust or fading means a full recoat is the better choice. We tell you which applies when we assess the part.

Not sure whether your part needs stripping at all? Send photos with your quote request. A restoration quote for powder coat stripping and recoating starts with a clear description of the damage and the finish you want, and it lets us refinish metal parts without guesswork. Whatever you choose, we confirm the plan with you before work starts.
How We Check Restoration Quality
For every powder coat stripping and recoating job, we check the bare metal after removal, then the finished coat, before parts leave the shop. Our quality steps are outlined on our
certification
page, and test reports are available on request.

Where a job calls for it, test methods include the ASTM D3359 adhesion test, ASTM D7091 for dry film thickness and ASTM B117 for salt spray resistance. Our certification is held through the Absolute Bureau of Certification. A new finish is only worth applying if it stays bonded, so we test adhesion as well as appearance on powder coat recoating work, which helps prevent a repeat adhesion failure or coating failure. We also confirm the cured finish is even, with no thin spots, runs or bare patches.
Restoration in Practice
Our
church gates

project shows how Koojo documents architectural metalwork from first inspection to the finished coat. The case study lists the part, metal, size, powder, colour code and turnaround, with before and after photos, so you can see how stripping and recoating work is recorded.
You can also browse more finished parts on our
Our Work

children.text: What Is Automotive Powder Coating?

Automotive powder coating is a dry finishing process in which electrostatically charged powder is sprayed onto metal vehicle parts, then heated in an oven until it melts and cures into a hard, even coating. It protects bare metal from rust, chips and everyday wear.

The finish is made from thermoset powder, which cures with heat instead of drying like liquid paint. At a cure temperature of 180 to 200 °C, the powder flows, bonds to the metal and hardens into one continuous layer without runs or drips. That makes it a dependable corrosion-resistant automotive coating for parts that face grit, moisture and impact, such as frames, brackets, suspension arms and underbody components. That is why vehicle powder coating is common on trucks and trailers that see winter road salt.
Typical customers include builders of custom motorcycles, owners of trucks and trailers, and shops that send out metal parts for finishing. If your project needs custom car parts powder coating, our
powder coating services
cover it from intake to handoff. Good auto parts powder coating also depends on the work done before the powder goes on, so we plan every job from the bare metal up.
Our Automotive Powder Coating Process

Our automotive powder coating process has six stages: intake and inspection, cleaning and pretreatment, masking, powder application, oven curing and final inspection. Each stage is documented so repeat orders match the first batch. The same controls support our
industrial powder coating
work.
Step 1 – Intake and Inspection

We check each part for heavy rust, old coatings, weld quality and damage, then confirm the finish you want for your automotive powder coating order. We also decide how to hang the part so every surface can be reached.
Step 2 – Cleaning and Pretreatment
Parts are washed and pretreated so the powder bonds to clean metal. Skipping this stage is a common reason rust protection for car parts fails early.
Step 3 – Masking and Plugging

Threads, bearing surfaces and mounting holes are protected before coating. Masking and plugging keep bolts turning and parts fitting, which matters on any valve cover powder coating or engine bracket powder coating order.
Step 4 – Electrostatic Powder Application
Charged powder is sprayed onto the grounded part, so it wraps around tubes, corners and recesses. Electrostatic powder application gives an even film across a complex frame.
Step 5 – Oven Curing

The part moves into the curing oven, where automotive powder coating reaches temperature and hardens. Cure time depends on the powder and the mass of the part, so a heavy chassis is planned differently from a small bracket.
Step 6 – Final Inspection and Handoff

We inspect the cured finish for coverage, adhesion and appearance. Typical orders are ready within 48 hours, and larger batch powder coating jobs are scheduled when we quote. We receive parts Monday to Friday, 7 AM to 5 PM.
Our automotive powder coating services schedule each stage so parts never wait between steps, and for car powder coating on a deadline, tell us your date at quote.
Parts and Metals We Coat
We apply automotive powder coating to steel, aluminum and cast parts, including frames, chassis components, brackets, valve covers and suspension parts. Our
capabilities
page lists 6,000 lb capacity, so heavy truck frames, trailer parts and other large vehicle components are worth a quote.
Frames: car frame powder coating and truck frame powder coating, full or partial.
Chassis and suspension: chassis powder coating, suspension parts powder coating and control arm powder coating.
Motorcycles: motorcycle frame powder coating and motorcycle parts powder coating for custom builds.
Body hardware: bumper powder coating, skid plate powder coating, running board powder coating and roll cage powder coating.
Heavy use: trailer hitch powder coating and off-road parts powder coating.
Wheels have their own dedicated process, so see our
wheel and rim powder coating
page for rims. Not sure what can be coated? Read
which car parts can be powder coated
, or send photos with your quote request.

Metals we handle: steel for frames and brackets, aluminum for lighter components, and cast parts such as covers and housings. Our powder coating for automotive parts starts with a material check at intake, because the right prep and cure plan depends on the metal and the thickness of the part.
Finish and Option Choices

Choose from gloss, satin, matte and textured finishes in a wide range of colours. We confirm the powder type, colour code and film thickness at quote, so the finish suits the part, the metal and how it will be used.

content.text: Gloss black powder coating and other high-gloss finishes give a deep, smooth look.
Matte black powder coating cuts glare and hides light scuffs.
Textured powder coating hides small surface marks and adds grip.
Typical film is 2 to 4 mils. We confirm mil thickness on fit-critical parts.
Chip-resistant powder coating forms a durable automotive finish for daily use.

children.text: Whatever you pick, vehicle powder coating should look consistent from part to part, so a matching frame and brackets leave the shop in one colour.

Film thickness affects fit, so tell us about tight tolerances before we coat. For a gloss, matte or textured automotive powder coating finish, send your colour code or a sample with your quote request.
Quality Standards for Automotive Powder Coating

Our automotive powder coating follows recognized standards: ASTM D3359 for adhesion, ASTM D7091 for dry film thickness and ASTM B117 for salt spray resistance. Koojo is certified through the Absolute Bureau of Certification, and test reports are available on request.

Quality starts at intake and ends at handoff. After curing, a good finish looks even in colour and gloss, with no thin spots, runs or bare edges. We flag any concern with you before parts leave the shop.

An ASTM D3359 adhesion test checks that the coating bonds to the metal. Dry film thickness readings confirm the coating is neither too thin to protect nor too thick to fit. The ASTM B117 salt spray test measures corrosion resistance in a controlled chamber. It is a comparison tool rather than a promise of real-world life, so we explain what results mean for your parts.

Batch inspection means each load is checked before parts leave the shop, which keeps repeat orders consistent and adds road salt protection you can rely on. Careful vehicle powder coating also depends on clean prep and correct curing, so every order follows the same documented steps. See our
certification
page for details.

children.text: What Is Rim Powder Coating?

Rim powder coating is a finishing process in which dry, electrostatically charged powder is sprayed onto a bare wheel and cured in an oven. The powder melts into a smooth, hard shell that suits both alloy rim powder coating and steel rim powder coating.

Unlike liquid paint, powder has no solvent carrier. The charged particles cling to the metal, then melt and cross-link in the oven, typically at 180 to 200 °C. That heat-driven reaction forms a continuous film that resists chipping better than most sprayed paint, which is why powder coated rims cope well with gravel, brake dust and winter road treatments.
People use wheel powder coating and powder coating wheels to describe the same job: refinishing the wheel itself. Frames, chassis and other vehicle parts belong to our
automotive powder coating
page. This page covers wheels only, from one set of cast aluminum wheels to repeat orders of steel wheel refinishing.

Why choose powder over paint? Rim powder coating applies in a single controlled booth, cures without a solvent carrier and leaves a finish that is thicker and more uniform than most spray cans or brush jobs. It also reaches spokes, lips and barrels evenly, which is hard to do by hand. For most owners, professional rim powder coating is the simpler route to a finish that lasts.
How Does Our Rim Powder Coating Process Work?

Our wheel powder coating process follows six stages: inspection, stripping, surface preparation, masking, powder application and oven curing. Each stage protects the metal, and every wheel is checked before it leaves our Milton shop.

Inspection (on arrival). We check each wheel for curb rash, cracks, bent lips and corrosion, and we note any old coating. Please bring wheels without tires, valve stems, pressure sensors or balance weights, because the oven heat would damage them. Clear notes about the finish you want help us quote accurately.
Wheel stripping. Old paint, clear coat or powder is removed so the new finish bonds to bare metal. Heavy corrosion may call for our
sandblasting services
before anything else happens.
Wheel surface preparation. Washing, degreasing and drying remove oil, brake dust and residue. Our
powder coating surface preparation
step is where a long-lasting finish is won or lost.
Masking. Wheel bolt hole masking, hub bore plugs and valve stem protection keep critical fitting surfaces clean, so the wheel still sits correctly on the vehicle.

Powder application. We spray your chosen colour electrostatically, reaching spokes, barrels and lips evenly. Clean, controlled application is the heart of rim powder coating, and it is why we keep this step separate from preparation.

Oven curing. The wheel cures at oven temperature, cools, and is inspected for coverage and smoothness. A full cure matters, because rim powder coating only reaches its strength once the powder has completely cross-linked.

Timing matters. Typical shop orders follow our standard 48-hour turnaround, and we receive wheels Monday to Friday, 7 AM to 5 PM. Forged wheel powder coating, two-tone wheels, heavy corrosion or large batches can need more time, so we confirm the schedule when we quote.
Which Wheels Suit Rim Powder Coating?

Most aluminum alloy and steel wheels suit rim powder coating, including cast and forged designs, provided they handle curing heat and have no serious cracks. Send photos and wheel details, and we will confirm suitability before any work starts.
Alloy wheels. Alloy wheel powder coating suits cast aluminum wheels and forged wheels. Cast aluminum can trap gases that cause pinholes, so we plan the preparation around the metal before coating.
Steel rims. Steel wheel refinishing removes rust and returns tired steel rims to a clean, uniform surface that resists new corrosion.
Other vehicles. We also take truck wheel powder coating, trailer wheel powder coating, ATV wheel powder coating and motorcycle wheel powder coating, whether you have one wheel or a full set.

To prepare for drop-off, remove loose dirt where you can, mark which wheel sits at which corner and take clear photos of any damage. Good photos let us quote rim powder coating accurately and spot issues early. We coat the surface, so structural wheel repair belongs with a qualified wheel specialist. If a wheel is bent or cracked, have it checked first and then send it to us. Our
capabilities page
lists size and weight limits for oversize wheels and heavy-duty wheel coating.
What Finishes Does Rim Powder Coating Offer?

Rim powder coating lets you choose gloss, satin, matte, textured, metallic or clear finishes, with colours matched to a RAL code or a physical sample. We help you pick a finish that suits the wheel design and how the vehicle is driven.
Popular looks. Matte black rims and gloss black wheels are common requests, and two-tone wheels add contrast between the face and the lip using careful masking.
Clear and metallic. A clear coat wheel finish adds depth over metallic powders and makes the colour pop.
Colour choice. Custom rim powder coating lets you move beyond stock colours. Our rim powder coating colours follow RAL references, and our
custom powder coating colours
page shows the wider range.
Matching. Need a factory colour match? Send a sample or colour code, and we will recommend the closest powder.

Not sure which finish fits? Send photos and tell us how the vehicle is used. Our wheel restoration advice comes with every quote, and we will flag anything that could affect the final look before we start. Ask for a colour sample if you want to compare finishes before you decide. A short chat before coating prevents surprises and keeps your project on schedule.
How Do We Check Rim Powder Coating Quality?

We inspect every rim before and after coating for even coverage, a smooth film, clean masked areas and a complete cure. Koojo is certified through the Absolute Bureau of Certification, and test reports are available on request.

Preparation drives results. Coating over clean, bare metal gives better wheel corrosion protection, because the cured film seals the surface against moisture. Good road salt protection depends on that same bond, so we never rush stripping or washing. Consistent coating also means the next set matches the last, because we keep records that support repeat orders.

A fully cured film also gives a chip-resistant wheel finish, while an under-cured one stays soft. The smooth surface offers a brake dust resistant finish too, since dust is easier to wipe away than from rough paint. Together, these steps create a durable wheel finish that keeps its look through changing seasons.
To keep your rims looking sharp, wash them with mild soap and a soft brush, and avoid harsh acid cleaners. See our
certification page
to learn how we document our work.
See Rim Powder Coating Preparation in a Real Project

Our safety bollards case study shows how we document a real metal project, from preparation and powder to colour code and turnaround. It is not a wheel job, but it shows the prep-first approach behind our rim powder coating.
Read the
safety bollards project

to see the standard we hold ourselves to. Before and after photos show the work from bare metal through to the finished coating, and the same documented approach applies to your wheels. For repeat orders, we can record the wheel type, metal and colour code so every batch matches the last.
Who Uses Our Rim Powder Coating?

Vehicle owners, trailer builders, farm and heavy equipment operators, contractors and fabrication shops send us wheels most often. They want rim powder coating that is dependable, fast and consistent from the first wheel to the last.
Trailer and equipment fleets suit
agricultural and heavy equipment

contractors and construction

industrial powder coating
work and the full range of
powder coating services
at our Milton shop. Whatever you drive or operate, we treat each rim as a precision part and plan the coating around how it will be used.

children.text: What Is Architectural Powder Coating?

Architectural powder coating is a finishing process in which dry, electrostatically charged powder is sprayed onto prepared building metalwork and cured in an oven. It forms a hard, even shell that protects the steel and aluminum parts used on and around buildings.

Unlike liquid paint, powder has no solvent carrier. The charged particles cling to the metal, then melt and cross-link in the oven, typically at 180 to 200 °C. That heat-driven reaction forms a continuous film that resists chipping, scratching and fading better than most sprayed paint, which is why powder coated railings and powder coated fences hold up well to weather.
The term architectural coatings covers finishes for building elements. This page focuses on exterior metal coating for railings, fences, gates and frames. Machinery and equipment belong to our
industrial powder coating
page, and vehicle parts have their own pages.

Why choose powder over paint for building metal? Architectural powder coating applies in a controlled booth, cures without a solvent carrier and gives a thicker, more uniform finish than most brush or spray paint. It also reaches welds, joints and tube ends evenly, which is hard to do by hand on site. For most projects, professional architectural powder coating is the simpler route to a finish that lasts.
How Does Our Architectural Powder Coating Process Work?

Our architectural powder coating process follows six stages: inspection, stripping or blasting, pretreatment, masking, powder application and oven curing. Each stage protects the metal, and every part is checked before it leaves our Milton shop.

Inspection (on arrival). We check each railing, frame or fence section for rust, weld spatter, old coatings and damage. Please remove glass, gaskets, plastic parts and any hardware that heat could harm. Clear notes on the colour and finish you want help us quote accurately.
Stripping and blasting. Old paint, powder or rust is removed so the new finish bonds to bare metal. Heavy rust or mill scale may call for our
sandblasting services
first.
Pretreatment. Washing, degreasing and rinsing remove oil, dirt and weld residue. Our
powder coating surface preparation
step is where an outdoor finish is won or lost.
Masking. Threaded holes, mounting faces and contact points are masked or plugged, so parts still fit and install cleanly on site.

Powder application. We spray your chosen colour electrostatically, reaching joints, tube ends and edges evenly. Clean, controlled application is the heart of architectural powder coating, and it is why we keep this step separate from preparation.
Oven curing. Each part cures at oven temperature, cools, and is inspected for coverage and smoothness before packing for pickup or delivery.

Timing matters. Typical shop orders follow our standard 48-hour turnaround, and we receive parts Monday to Friday, 7 AM to 5 PM. Long railing runs, heavy rust, several colours or large batches can need more time, so we confirm the schedule when we quote. We pack finished parts carefully for pickup or delivery to your site.
Which Parts Suit Architectural Powder Coating?

Most steel and aluminum building components suit architectural powder coating, including railings, fences, gates and frames, provided they fit our oven and handle curing heat. Send photos and dimensions, and we will confirm suitability before work starts.

Railings and stairs. Stair railing powder coating, balcony railing powder coating and handrail powder coating protect welded joints and tube ends, where weather attacks first. Aluminum railing powder coating suits lighter systems.

Fences and gates. Fence powder coating and gate powder coating suit steel and aluminum sections. Aluminum fence powder coating keeps lightweight panels uniform, while steel fence finishing seals the metal against rust.

children.text: What Is Commercial Powder Coating?

Commercial powder coating is a dry finishing process in which electrostatically charged powder is sprayed onto metal parts, then heated in an oven until it cures into a hard, even layer. It suits business orders where many parts must match, resist wear and ship on schedule.

The finish is made from thermoset powder, which cures with heat instead of drying like liquid paint. At a cure temperature of 180 to 200 °C, the powder flows, bonds to the metal and hardens into one continuous coating without runs or drips. As a form of commercial metal finishing, it replaces liquid paint where durability and repeatability matter. That makes it a dependable corrosion-resistant and chip-resistant choice for parts that face handling, weather and wear.

Typical customers send fabricated metal parts and commercial equipment components that must look alike from the first piece to the last. A commercial-grade finish should look the same on part one and part five hundred. Strong production powder coating depends on repeatable steps, so our commercial powder coating is planned around the whole order, starting from the bare metal. Our wider
powder coating services

Our Commercial Powder Coating Process

Our commercial powder coating process has six stages: intake and inspection, cleaning and pretreatment, masking, powder application, oven curing and final inspection. Each stage is documented so reorders match the first batch. The same controls support our
industrial powder coating
work.
Step 1 – Intake and Inspection

We check each part for heavy rust, old coatings, weld quality and damage, then confirm the finish, quantity and delivery date for your order. We also plan racking so every surface can be reached and each load holds as many parts as it safely can.
Step 2 – Cleaning and Pretreatment
Parts are washed and chemically treated so the powder bonds to clean metal. Skipping this stage is a common reason finishes fail early. For more on this stage, see our
powder coating surface preparation
page.
Step 3 – Masking and Plugging

Threads, bearing surfaces and mounting holes are protected before coating. Masking and plugging keep bolts turning and parts fitting, which matters when hundreds of identical parts must assemble without rework.
Step 4 – Electrostatic Powder Application
Charged powder is applied by electrostatic spray onto the grounded part, so it wraps around tubes, corners and recesses. This gives an even film across every piece in the run.
Step 5 – Oven Curing

Parts move into the curing oven, where commercial powder coating reaches temperature and hardens. Cure time depends on the powder and the mass of the part, so a heavy frame is planned differently from a small bracket.
Step 6 – Final Inspection and Handoff

We inspect the cured finish for coverage, adhesion and appearance. Typical orders are ready within 48 hours, and larger production runs are scheduled when we quote. We receive parts Monday to Friday, 7 AM to 5 PM. We also record the colour and powder used, so a later order can repeat the finish exactly.

children.text: Coating Challenges for Metal Fabricators and Welding Shops

The main coating challenges for fabricators are weld seams, spatter, mixed metal thickness, sharp edges and tight deadlines. Each can cause thin spots, pinholes or rework without planning. Powder coating for metal fabricators works best when the weld is treated as part of the finish.

Welds are rough and often porous, and they heat differently from the sheet beside them. Weld spatter leaves bumps that show through the coating. Weld porosity traps air, which oven heat can push out as outgassing and leave blisters. Sharp edges pull the coating thin, so edge coverage needs attention on cut plate and tube ends. A heavy base plate welded to thin sheet also heats unevenly in the oven. Add the deadlines your own customers set, and finishing often becomes the bottleneck. Good powder coating for fabricators removes these risks before parts reach the oven, which keeps fabricated metal parts moving. Fabricator powder coating also has to cope with mixed shapes, sizes and metals, often in the same batch.
Choosing powder coating for metal fabricators with a documented prep routine protects your reputation as well as the part, because a failed finish comes back to the shop that built the frame.

content.text: Conveyor frame for a production line

children.text: The Challenge

The challenge was to give an automotive conveyor frame a finish that survives daily production-line wear, covers every weld and inside corner evenly, keeps bolt-on points bare, and returns in time for the plant's installation date.

Conveyor frames in automotive plants work hard. They carry fixtures and parts through every shift, get bumped by carts and forklifts, and are wiped down with degreasers during cleaning. A thin or poorly bonded coating chips at the edges first, and rust then creeps in at the welds. For OEM conveyor frames, a failed finish means stripping and recoating, which brings unplanned downtime that no plant wants. Edges, welds and fixture contact points are the areas most at risk.

A welded conveyor frame also brings its own prep problems. The fabricated frame structure carries mill scale and weld spatter that block adhesion. Machined mounting faces and threaded holes must stay bare so the frame bolts into the line without rework. That is why this automotive plant conveyor frame case study starts with the problem rather than the powder. Those are the details a coater has to plan for before quoting.

Timing mattered as much as quality. Installs like this are tied to the plant shutdown schedule, so the conveyor frame turnaround could not slip on this conveyor frame project. The size of the automotive plant conveyor frame also called for planned space in our large oven rather than a standard batch slot.
Our Approach

Our approach in this automotive plant conveyor frame case study followed one controlled sequence: prepare the metal, apply the powder electrostatically, then cure and inspect the finish. Each step was set for the frame's size, its welds and the plant's finish specification.
Preparation

We started by checking the drawing and the plant's finish spec, confirming the specified colour code and marking every surface that had to stay uncoated. Abrasive blast cleaning then handled mill scale removal and welding spatter removal in one pass, leaving a blast profile for powder coating so the finish had something to grip. Next came degreasing and a phosphate pretreatment for steel, followed by a rinse and a full dry so no moisture stayed in seams or tube ends. Masking machined surfaces and masking threaded holes came last, keeping every bolt-on point clean. Open tube ends were checked so pretreatment liquid could drain and dry fully. Much of an automotive conveyor frame's service life is decided at this stage.
Application

Electrostatic powder application charges the powder so it wraps around tubes and into inside corners. On this conveyor frame project, that gave even coverage over welds and edges, the places where chips usually start on assembly line equipment. We racked the frame so powder could reach every face and kept film build consistent from flat panels to corners. Hanging points were chosen where marks would not show once the frame was installed. A durable powder finish depends on that coverage as much as on the powder itself.
Curing & Inspection

Large part oven curing at 180–200 °C, following the powder maker's cure schedule, cross-linked the powder into a hard, chip resistant finish. Our oven handles parts up to 6,000 lb, so the heaviest sections of the automotive plant conveyor frame cured with the rest. We then ran a dry film thickness check to ASTM D7091 on faces, edges and welds, plus a cross hatch adhesion test to ASTM D3359. Readings focus on edges and welds because those are the first places a thin coat would show. Every reading went into the job file, which keeps this automotive plant conveyor frame case study verifiable. Standard orders run on a 48 hour turnaround, and the actual time for the automotive conveyor frame is shown in the snapshot.
The Result

The result was a fully coated automotive conveyor frame with an even, chip resistant finish over every weld and edge, clean bolt-on points, and thickness and adhesion readings on file for the plant's quality records.

Because the masked faces on the automotive plant conveyor frame stayed bare, it could be bolted straight into the line with no grinding on site. Film build stayed consistent from flat faces to inside corners, which matters most where carts and fixtures strike the frame. Good conveyor system frame finishing like this means fewer touch-ups and less downtime between shutdowns. The cured finish also wipes clean during routine plant washdowns.

A colour matched equipment finish keeps the line consistent with the plant's other equipment, and corrosion resistant frame coating at the welds protects the joints that carry the most load. This conveyor frame case study reflects the same standard we apply to all automotive plant equipment coating.

If your line needs the same result, use this automotive plant conveyor frame case study as a benchmark when you compare quotes. Ask any coater for the prep method, test readings and a powder coated frame you can inspect, not just a price. Plant maintenance teams also gain a clear record: the colour code, powder and readings are stored, so a replacement frame or an added section can be matched later without guesswork.

content.text: Welded machine frame for an automated assembly line

children.text: The Challenge

The challenge was to coat an automation line frame so it resists factory floor wear while its mounting plates, tapped holes and grounding points stay bare, flat and ready for equipment to bolt on without any rework at line commissioning.
That is why this automation line frame case study begins with what had to stay uncoated rather than with the colour.

An automated cell is only as accurate as the frame under it. Robots, vision sensors and fixtures bolt onto flat mounting plates, and any coating left on those faces can throw alignment off or stop a bracket from seating. Tight tolerance holes have the same problem, because powder in a thread or a dowel bore means drilling or tapping on site.

Electrical continuity added another layer. Automation equipment needs a clean path to ground, and a coated contact point breaks it. Grounding point masking therefore had to be planned on the drawing, not left to the person spraying. Getting that wrong on one frame would mean a call from the integrator during start-up, which is the risk this automation frame case study sets out to avoid.

Appearance mattered too. Machine builder frames are often built as modular frame sections that sit side by side, so every piece had to match the client's equipment colour standard. Batch colour consistency across the sections was part of the brief, along with a production schedule that left little slack for this automation line frame project.
Our Approach

Our approach in this automation line frame case study ran in three stages: masking and surface prep, an even electrostatic coat, and a cure followed by checks of every bare surface. The masking plan came first, because the bare surfaces decided how the rest of the job was run.
Preparation

We marked every mounting plate, tapped hole and grounding point on the drawing with the client before work began. Media blasting cleaned the welds and removed scale so the powder had a sound surface to bond to, and chemical pretreatment followed to improve adhesion and corrosion resistance. The frame was rinsed and dried fully before masking. On precision frames, masking often takes longer than spraying itself. Welds were also checked for porosity before blasting, since trapped air can cause pinholes during cure. Heat-resistant plugs filled the tight tolerance holes, and high-temperature tape covered the sensor mounting surfaces and ground pads. Careful prep is what turns an automation line frame into an install-ready frame.
Application

Electrostatic spraying carried the powder around tube corners and into gussets, giving weld seam coverage and edge coverage without heavy build on the flat faces. We set hang points away from visible surfaces and turned the frame during spraying so every side received the same film. Spray settings stayed the same for every section of the frame for an automation line, which keeps gloss and texture matched. Film build uniformity matters on modular frames, because a thicker coat on one section can show as a colour or gloss shift beside its neighbour on this automation line frame project.
Curing & Inspection

Curing ran at 180–200 °C on the thermoset powder supplier's oven cure cycle, in an oven rated for parts up to 6,000 lb. After cooling, we removed the masking and checked every bare surface for clean edges, with the drawing in hand so nothing was missed. Film thickness readings were taken to ASTM D7091 and adhesion testing was done to ASTM D3359, and the results sit in the job file. Those records keep this automation line frame case study traceable. Our usual 48 hour turnaround applies to standard work; the snapshot shows how long the automation line frame actually took.
The Result

The result was a powder coated machine frame with a smooth industrial finish, clean mounting plates and grounding points, open threads and recorded test readings, ready for the integrator to fit equipment as soon as the automation line frame arrived.

Because the masked areas stayed bare, robots and sensors could be bolted down and grounded without scraping or re-tapping. Even film build kept the frame square to the drawing, and the matched colour let it sit beside other sections without a visible change. That saves time at line commissioning, which is often the tightest part of an automation schedule.

The coating also protects the frame from the knocks, coolant splash and cleaning it will see over years of service. This automation frame case study shows the standard we bring to all automation equipment frame coating, whether the order is one frame or multi-frame orders for a full line. Maintenance teams also get a record of the powder and colour code, so a replacement section for the automation line frame can be matched later.

content.text: Welded line frame for a food processing line (non-food-contact) [confirm]

children.text: The Challenge

The challenge was to give a food processing line frame a washdown resistant finish that stays intact through daily cleaning, never chips into the production area, and keeps rust away from welds in a space that is wet for most of every shift.

Food plants are tough on coatings. Lines are rinsed with hot water, scrubbed with sanitation chemicals and often hit with high-pressure washdown at the end of each run. Moisture and condensation stay on the frame long after cleaning, so any weak spot in the coating soon turns into rust at a weld or a cut edge. Each weld on the food processing line frame had to be treated as a possible failure point.

The bigger concern is contamination risk. A chip of coating that falls near product is a quality problem, and plant hygiene audits look closely at flaking paint, rust and rough surfaces that trap residue. Chip and flake resistance therefore mattered as much as appearance. That is why this food processing line frame case study starts with hygiene rather than colour.

The frame itself added detail. Its support legs and cross members carry many welds and cut edges, each a place where a thin coat would fail first. Carbon steel frame coating is a common stainless steel alternative for non-food-contact parts, but only when the finish is complete, so full coverage was the goal on this food processing line frame project.
Our Approach

Our approach in this food processing line frame case study had three stages: prepare the steel for a wet environment, apply the powder with full edge and weld coverage, then cure and verify the finish before it went anywhere near the plant.
Preparation

We reviewed the drawing and the plant's requirements with the client first, including where the frame would sit and what it would be cleaned with. Blasting stripped scale and rust back to clean steel that was ready for bonding. Sharp weld spatter was ground back to give smooth weld transitions, because a rough bead is hard to clean and easy to chip. Chemical pretreatment then improved adhesion and corrosion protection in wet areas, and the frame was rinsed and dried right through, including inside every seam. Masking was kept to bolt holes and mounting pads, so the food processing line frame project kept as much protected surface as possible. Preparation like this decides how long a food processing line frame lasts.
Application

Powder selection came before spraying. We agreed on a chemical resistant powder suited to the cleaning regime, and the client chose the colour and gloss level; many plants prefer a light colour finish because residue is easier to spot. Electrostatic spraying then gave strong edge wrap on cut ends and full coverage on welds and inside corners. Hang points were placed away from surfaces that would be visible in service, and the frame was turned so every face of the frame for a food processing line received the same film.
Curing & Inspection

We baked the frame at 180–200 °C for the time the powder's data sheet specifies; the oven can handle items weighing as much as 6,000 lb. Once cool, it went through coating thickness verification under ASTM D7091 across flat panels, corners and weld lines, and an adhesion check under ASTM D3359, with each reading logged to the job. Those records keep this food processing line frame case study traceable for the plant's own audits. For timing, standard jobs leave in 48 hours, and the real figure for the food processing line frame is listed in the snapshot table.
The Result

The plant received a food processing line frame with a cleanable smooth finish, complete coverage on every weld and cut end, and test data in its file, ready to return to a wet processing area without chipping or early rust.

A hygienic finish like this helps sanitation crews clean faster, because residue wipes off a smooth surface instead of sitting in pits and rough welds. Good moisture resistance at the edges protects the frame between cleans, which supports processing line uptime and keeps maintenance off the schedule.

The light, even colour also makes the frame easier to inspect during a sanitation shift. content.text: Welded robot pedestal / riser for a robotic cell

children.text: The Challenge

The challenge was to put a durable industrial coating on a heavy robotic base while keeping the machined top plate, the bolt pattern and the anchor bolt holes completely bare, so the robot and the floor fixings would seat exactly as designed.

A floor-mounted robot transfers its dynamic loads straight into the pedestal below it. Every fast move of the arm flexes and shakes the steel, and any coating trapped under the robot flange can creep or crack over time. That is why the top mounting plate needs true metal-to-metal contact, with no powder between the robot and the steel. Every one of those features on the robotic base had a job to do once the cell was running.

The underside brought the same issue. Levelling pads and anchor bolts set the base square to the floor, and powder in those holes would mean drilling or grinding on site during robot installation. Cable pass-through openings also had to stay clean so grommets would fit. Planning those details first is why this robotic base case study opens with what had to stay uncoated.

Then there was the mass. Thick steel sections heat slowly in an oven, so a base like this cannot simply share a cycle with thin sheet parts. It also had to survive forklift handling in the plant and arrive for the integrator's delivery date, which left little room for error on this robotic base project.
Our Approach

Our approach in this robotic base case study followed three steps: blast and mask the heavy steel, spray a uniform coat, then bring the whole mass up to its true part temperature and test the result. The masking plan and the cure plan were fixed before any blasting started.
Preparation

We marked the machined top plate, the bolt pattern, the anchor holes on the robotic base and the cable openings on the drawing with the client. Abrasive blasting took mill scale and weld spatter off the heavy plate steel, giving the powder a rough, clean profile to key into. After a chemical pretreatment, the base was rinsed and left to dry completely. Thread protection came next: heat-resistant plugs went into every tapped hole and high-temperature tape covered the mounting faces. Welds on thick plate can hold air, so preheating was used, where needed, to drive off any outgassing before powder went on.
Application

Electrostatic spraying carried the powder over gussets, welds and edges, the areas most exposed to bumps around a robotic cell. We hung the welded steel pedestal from points that would sit out of sight once installed, and turned it during spraying so every face of the robotic base received the same film. Hanging points were also checked so the pedestal could not swing into other parts while it was sprayed. Even coverage on the column and feet protects the base where carts and forklifts are most likely to strike it, and keeps the colour consistent with the cell colour scheme.
Curing & Inspection

Heavy parts are cured by part temperature, not just oven time. The robotic base stayed in our oven until the steel itself reached the 180–200 °C cure range set by the powder maker, which matters on thick sections that lag behind the air. Pieces weighing up to 6,000 lb fit in that oven. Once it had cooled, the tape and plugs came out and each mounting face was inspected. Cure verification included readings with a film thickness gauge to ASTM D7091 and a cross-cut adhesion test to ASTM D3359, all recorded against the job number. Those records keep this robotic base case study traceable. Typical orders are done in 48 hours, and the snapshot records the exact duration of this robotic base project.
The Result

The client got back a robot riser with strong impact resistance on the column and feet, a bare top plate ready for the robot flange, open anchor and tapped holes, and recorded test readings for the integrator's file.

Because the mounting faces on the robotic base stayed clean, the robot could be bolted down and torqued without scraping or re-tapping, and the base sat level on its pads. Full cure through the thick sections means the coating will not soften or mark under load, which protects the finish where the arm's movement is felt most. Clean seating also shortens commissioning, usually the tightest part of a robot project.

The finish also guards against corrosion from coolant, cleaning and the humidity of a working plant. This robotic base case study reflects the standard we bring to every heavy machine base, whether the order is a single pedestal or a run of matching pedestals for a new line. Careful packaging for transport protected the finished faces of the robotic base project on the way out.

children.text: The Challenge

The challenge was to give each safety bollard in the batch a high-visibility finish that stays bright under constant outdoor exposure, resists rust from road salt and survives knocks from vehicles, carts and snowplows for years without regular repainting.

Bollards work in one of the harshest settings a coating can face. Summer sun breaks down weak finishes and causes colour fade and chalking, while winter brings freeze-thaw cycles and salt spray from passing traffic. Once water gets under a chip, corrosion undercutting spreads beneath the coating and lifts it away from the steel. A safety bollard that turns rusty and dull also stops doing its job of being seen. Ontario sites see both extremes within the same year.

Impact is the other test. Vehicle impact from bumpers, shopping carts and snowplow damage all hit the same band near the top of each post, so the coating needs real toughness as well as weather resistance. Any weak point at the welds, the caps or the cut edges at the base would fail first. That is why this bollard powder coating case study begins with where the posts will stand.

Consistency mattered too. A row of posts outside a building is seen side by side, so every piece needed the same shade and gloss. The client also needed the posts back in time for site installation, so the schedule for this bollard powder coating project had to hold.
Our Approach

Our approach in this bollard powder coating case study was built around three steps: get the steel ready for years outdoors, spray a weather-rated powder, then cure and check each post before it went to site.
Preparation

We checked the drawing and the site specification with the client first, including the colour, the expected exposure and whether any posts were removable bollards with sleeves that had to stay uncoated. Abrasive blasting removed mill scale, rust and weld spatter from the steel pipe bollards and left a clean profile for the powder to grip. After chemical pretreatment and rinsing, each post was dried inside and out, including under the base plates. Posts with welded base plates need extra care at that joint, where water tends to collect. Drain holes were checked so water could not sit inside a post after installation. Where a project calls for extra corrosion protection, a zinc-rich primer can be added before the topcoat; whether this order used one is recorded in the specs. Careful prep is what keeps a safety bollard finish from lifting at the base.
Application

Powder choice comes first for outdoor work. For posts like these we use an outdoor polyester powder, a UV resistant powder type made to hold colour in direct sun, in the colour the client specified. Electrostatic spraying wrapped the powder around the pipe, over the welds and onto the bollard caps and base plates, with extra attention to cut edges. Each safety bollard hung from a point that would be hidden once installed, and the whole batch of matching bollards was sprayed with the same settings for a consistent colour match.
Curing & Inspection

The batch went through the oven together at 180–200 °C, timed to the manufacturer's data, and since the oven accepts loads up to 6,000 lb, long or heavy posts fit in one cycle. After cooling, each safety bollard was checked for full coverage and even colour. Thickness readings followed ASTM D7091, the adhesion test followed ASTM D3359, and both sets of numbers were filed with the order. Those records keep this bollard powder coating case study traceable. We quote 48 hours for standard work, and how long this bollard powder coating project took is noted in the snapshot.
The Result

The result was a set of safety bollards with a bright, even, weather-ready finish, full coverage over welds, caps and base plates, a consistent colour match across every post, and test readings on file, ready for site installation.

A low-maintenance finish like this cuts the cost of owning bollards. Instead of yearly scraping and repainting, the coating keeps rust out and stays visible through Ontario winters and summers. That matters for pedestrian protection, because a faded, rusty post is easy to miss at night or in snow. Each bollard powder coating project we finish is planned for that kind of service life.

The same standard applies to parking lot bollards, loading dock bollards and base plate bollards used for storefront protection. Many sites add reflective bands after coating, and a sound finish gives that tape a clean surface to hold. children.text: The Challenge

The task was to restore weathered metalwork with fine, curved detail: strip years of old paint and rust, reach deep into every scroll and joint with fresh powder, keep the hinges and latches working, and return a traditional look that suits the building.

Old church gates usually carry several layers of paint, each one applied over the last whenever the metal started to show rust. Those layers crack, trap moisture and hide rust pitting underneath. Simply painting over them again would only restart the repaint cycle, with flaking back within a few seasons. Each layer added to the problem rather than solving it, and the gate leaves on these church gates were no exception.

Shape added the real difficulty. Decorative scrollwork, pickets and finials create recessed corners and tight gaps where powder struggles to reach, a problem known as the faraday cage effect. Without care, the outer curves get a heavy coat while the inside of each scroll gets almost none, and that is where rust returns first. For this church gates case study, fine detail coverage was the main test.

Function and appearance also mattered. Hinges, latch hardware and any moving parts had to swing freely after coating, and the finish had to respect the heritage appearance of the church grounds. The client also wanted a short gap between gate removal and reinstallation, so the church gates project had to keep moving through each stage.
Our Approach

In this church gates case study the work followed three steps: strip and clean the metal back to bare steel, build the powder into every recess with careful spraying, then cure and inspect each leaf in good light before the gates went back to the church.
Preparation

Old paint removal came first. Layers that blasting alone would struggle with were stripped, and abrasive blasting then took the gates down to bare metal cleaning standard, opening up any rust pitting so it could be treated rather than hidden. We looked closely at every weld and scroll on the gates for a church for cracks or thin metal and flagged anything that needed repair before coating. Stripping also showed exactly how much original metal remained. A chemical pretreatment came next, followed by a rinse and a thorough dry. Hinge masking and masking moving parts finished the prep, so pins and latches would turn freely once the church gates were rehung.
Application

Detailed metalwork needs a different spray technique from flat panels. We lowered the gun settings and worked into the scrolls first, letting the powder settle into recessed corners before coating the outer faces, which beats the faraday cage effect without piling up film on the edges. Colour sample approval came before spraying: the client chose a satin black finish, a low gloss finish that reads as traditional ironwork. Each leaf of the church gates was hung so contact marks would sit on hidden edges, and the gate posts were coated in the same batch so the set matches.
Curing & Inspection

The leaves cured at 180–200 °C to the powder supplier's schedule, in an oven that takes pieces up to 6,000 lb. When they had cooled, we checked inside scrolls and behind pickets with a light, where thin spots would hide, then measured thickness to ASTM D7091 and adhesion to ASTM D3359, logging every reading for the church gates project. Masking came off last, and each hinge and latch was worked by hand to confirm free movement. Work like this usually fits our 48 hour standard, and the snapshot notes how long this church gates case study actually took.
The Result

The church received its ornamental gates back with a smooth, even finish deep inside every scroll and joint, hinges and latches that swing freely, a colour that suits the building, and test readings on file for the parish property records.

Because the coating on these church gates reaches the recesses as well as the outer faces, there are no thin spots waiting to rust through. That breaks the cycle of scraping and repainting that older wrought iron gates often fall into, and it gives the church outdoor durability measured in years rather than seasons. Maintenance drops to an occasional wash.

Visually, the low sheen hides small marks and keeps the gates close to the look of traditional ironwork. Visitors see clean, crisp detail on the finials and pickets instead of drips or heavy edges. The same restoration coating approach suits any church gates with fine detail, from a single garden gate to a full set of entrance leaves and posts. That is the standard we hold every church gates project to.

If your church or school is weighing up repainting against powder coating, this church gates case study is a fair guide to what to ask. Find out how the coater will remove old paint, how they will reach inside the scrollwork and how they will protect the hinges. The answers usually separate a lasting finish from another short repaint.
Specs at a Glance

Four details sum up the technical side of this church gates project: film thickness, prep grade, powder type and cure. Committees and contractors can share them with an architect or heritage adviser before deciding on their own gates.

data.title: What is Powder Coating?
data.excerpt: Powder coating is a dry finishing process used to apply a durable and attractive coating to surfaces, mostly metal.

children.text: Powder coating is a dry finishing process used to apply a durable and attractive coating to surfaces, mostly metal. Unlike traditional paint, it uses a dry powder made of pigment and resin, which is sprayed onto the surface using electrostatic charge. The item is then baked in an oven, where the powder melts and forms a smooth, hard finish.

Before coating, the surface is thoroughly cleaned to ensure proper adhesion. Once cured, the coating is resistant to scratches, fading, and corrosion. Powder coating is also environmentally friendly, as it contains no harmful solvents and produces minimal waste.

This method is widely used on car parts, appliances, outdoor furniture, and more. Its durability, variety of colors and finishes, and eco-friendliness make it a popular alternative to traditional painting.

data.title: Why Powder Coating is Ideal?
data.excerpt: There are numerous reasons why powder coating is an excellent finishing choice.

children.text: There are numerous reasons why powder coating is an excellent finishing choice. To begin with, it is far more durable than traditional paint and resists chips, scratches, and fading. This makes it ideal for car parts, outdoor furniture, and metal equipment. Furthermore, it helps protect against rust and wear, meaning everything coated is likely to last much longer. In addition to all that, there is another significant benefit—it's easier to apply. With powder coating, there are no uneven runs or drips, unlike paint. It is also more environmentally friendly. There are no noxious fumes or chemicals released and any excess powder is easily collected and reused, greatly reducing waste.

Aside from being tough and eco-friendly, it is also offered in a wide variety of colors and textures. For finishing touches, powder coating cures evenly and quickly under heat, making the entire application efficient. In any case, whether it’s a big manufacturing project or simply outdoor equipment, the coating provides a smart, long-lasting beauty.

data.title: The Powder Coating Process Step by Step: From Prep to Cure
data.excerpt: See the full powder coating process step by step, from surface prep and electrostatic application to oven curing, explained clearly for first-time customers

children.text: Understanding the
powder coating process step by step

helps demystify what actually happens to your part between drop-off and pickup, and why proper preparation matters just as much as the coating itself. Skipping or rushing any single stage can compromise the final finish, regardless of how good the powder or equipment is.

This guide walks through exactly how professional powder coating works, from initial surface preparation through final curing, so manufacturers, fabricators, and first-time customers across the Greater Toronto Area know exactly what to expect before requesting a quote.
How Does Powder Coating Work: The Basic Concept

Before diving into individual steps, it helps to understand how does powder coating work at a fundamental level. Unlike wet paint, which is a liquid applied and left to air-dry, powder coating uses a dry, finely ground powder that's electrically charged and sprayed onto a grounded metal surface. The charged particles are drawn evenly across the part, then the entire piece is baked in an oven, where the powder melts and chemically fuses into a hard, continuous film.

This combination of electrostatic application and heat curing is what gives powder coating its signature durability and even coverage, both of which depend heavily on getting each preceding step right.
Powder Coating Surface Preparation Steps: Where Quality Begins

The powder coating surface preparation steps that happen before any powder is ever applied arguably matter more than any other stage in the entire process. Improperly prepared surfaces are the leading cause of coating failure, regardless of how well the actual application and curing steps are executed.

Preparation typically begins with a thorough inspection of the part, followed by removal of any existing paint, rust, oil, or contaminants through methods like sandblasting, chemical stripping, or media blasting, depending on the part's condition and base material. This stage sets the foundation for everything that follows, since powder coating simply cannot bond properly to a dirty or contaminated surface.
Powder Coating Pretreatment Steps: Building the Adhesion Foundation

Following initial cleaning, powder coating pretreatment steps prepare the metal surface at a chemical level to maximize coating adhesion and long-term durability. This typically involves a multi-stage wash process, including degreasing, rinsing, and often a phosphate or chromate conversion coating that creates a microscopically textured surface for the powder to bond with more effectively.

Skipping or rushing pretreatment is one of the most common reasons powder coating fails prematurely, since even a visually clean surface can retain microscopic contaminants or lack the chemical profile needed for genuinely strong, long-term adhesion.
Powder Coating Application Process: Getting the Powder On
Once properly prepared, the
powder coating

application process begins with loading the specific powder formulation into an electrostatic spray gun. As the powder passes through the gun, it receives an electrical charge, causing the particles to be strongly attracted to the grounded metal part, wrapping around edges and into recessed areas more evenly than traditional spray methods typically achieve.

Technicians apply the powder in controlled passes, monitoring thickness and coverage to ensure the part receives a consistent coat without excessive buildup in any single area, since uneven application can lead to inconsistent curing and finish quality.
Electrostatic Powder Coating Process: Why This Method Works So Well

Understanding the electrostatic powder coating process specifically explains why powder coating achieves such reliable, even coverage compared to conventional painting. The electrical charge applied to the powder particles causes them to actively seek out the grounded metal surface, including areas that might otherwise be difficult to reach with a direct spray angle.

This physics-based attraction is also what allows overspray powder to be collected and reused in many operations, reducing material waste in a way that liquid paint overspray simply cannot match, since captured wet paint overspray typically can't be reclaimed for reuse.
Powder Coating Curing Process: Where the Finish Becomes Permanent

The powder coating curing process transforms the applied powder from a loosely adhered coating into a hard, permanent finish. Once the part is fully and evenly coated, it moves into a curing oven, where controlled heat causes the powder particles to melt, flow together, and chemically cross-link into a continuous, durable film.

This curing stage is what gives powder coating its exceptional durability compared to air-dried wet paint, since the heat-activated chemical bonding creates a molecular structure that's significantly more resistant to chipping, fading, and chemical exposure than a simply dried paint film.
Powder Coating Oven Curing Temperature: Getting the Details Right

Powder coating oven curing temperature typically ranges between 350°F and 400°F (roughly 175°C to 200°C), though the exact temperature and cure time depend on the specific powder formulation being used. Curing generally takes between 10 and 20 minutes once the part reaches the target temperature throughout, meaning larger or thicker parts may require longer oven time to ensure the core of the metal reaches curing temperature, not just the surface.

Getting this temperature and timing right matters significantly, since under-curing leaves the coating soft and prone to damage, while excessive heat or time can cause discoloration or brittleness in the finished film.
Powder Coating Process Explained: Putting It All Together
With each individual stage covered, the powder coating process explained as a complete sequence looks like this:
Inspection and cleaning
— Removing contamination, rust, or old coatings from the part
Pretreatment
— Chemical washing and conversion coating to maximize adhesion
Electrostatic application
— Spraying charged powder onto the grounded, prepared surface
Curing
— Baking the coated part in an oven to melt and chemically bond the finish
Cooling and inspection
— Allowing the part to cool before a final quality check
Each stage depends directly on the one before it, which is why working with an
experienced powder coating provider
who maintains quality control at every step matters just as much as the equipment itself.
Steps Involved in Powder Coating: Common Questions About Timing

Understanding the full steps involved in powder coating also helps set realistic expectations for turnaround time. Standard projects typically move through preparation, application, and curing within a single day for smaller batches, though larger or more heavily corroded parts requiring extensive surface preparation can extend the overall timeline meaningfully.
Custom color matching or specialty finishes may also add time, since achieving the exact right formulation sometimes requires additional testing before full production begins.
Powder Coating vs Traditional Painting Process: Key Process Differences

Comparing powder coating vs traditional painting process reveals why the two methods produce such different results. Traditional wet painting relies on solvent evaporation for drying, a process that happens at room temperature and can take considerably longer to fully cure, with the finish remaining relatively soft compared to a heat-cured powder coat. Powder coating's oven-curing process compresses this timeline dramatically while producing a chemically bonded, significantly harder finish.

This process difference is also why powder coating generally isn't suitable for materials that can't withstand oven temperatures, such as certain plastics or heat-sensitive components, situations where traditional wet painting remains the more practical choice.
Frequently Asked Questions
1. Why is surface preparation considered the most important step in powder coating?

Improper surface preparation is the leading cause of coating failure, since powder coating cannot properly bond to contaminated, rusted, or improperly cleaned surfaces, regardless of how well later steps are executed.
2. How long does the entire powder coating process typically take?
Standard projects often move through preparation, application, and curing within a single day, though heavily corroded parts or custom color matching can extend the timeline.
3. What happens if a part isn't cured at the right temperature?
Under-curing leaves the coating soft and prone to damage, while excessive heat or overly long curing can cause discoloration or brittleness in the finished film.
4. Can all metal parts go through the full curing oven process?
Most metals handle standard curing temperatures well, but parts with heat-sensitive components or certain non-metal attachments may require special handling or alternative finishing methods.
5. Why does powder coating produce a more even finish than spray painting?

The electrostatic charge applied during application causes powder particles to be actively attracted to the grounded metal surface, providing more consistent coverage, including into recessed areas, than gravity-dependent spray painting typically achieves.
Final Thoughts on the Powder Coating Process

Understanding the powder coating process step by step, from thorough surface preparation through precise oven curing, makes it clear why proper execution at every stage matters so much for the finished product's durability and appearance. Working with a provider that maintains quality control throughout the entire sequence ensures your parts receive the full benefit of what powder coating is genuinely capable of delivering.
